title: PoSTCache: From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing for Revisable Diffusion Caching

paper.title: PoSTCache: From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing for Revisable Diffusion Caching
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion and flow matching models achieve impressive visual generation quality but remain computationally expensive due to iterative sampling. Caching-based acceleration provides a practical training-free solution by reusing or predicting intermediate features. However, existing methods largely enforce a forward-only information flow: approximations produced for skipped model evaluations are immediately committed to the sampling trajectory and cannot benefit from feedback generated by later full-computation steps. We propose PoSTCache ( Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache ), a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. PoSTCache first uses an existing caching strategy to construct forward proposals for skipped steps. At a later full-computation step, the discrepancy between the refreshed prediction and its forward proposal yields a correction signal, which PoSTCache propagates backward to refine and reintegrate the preceding predictions. Viewing full-computation steps as sources of corrective feedback also changes how they should be selected. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and selects anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty rather than local approximation error alone. Experiments on representative image and video generation models show that PoSTCache consistently improves the quality–efficiency trade-off over representative caching methods.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020b ) and flow matching models ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) have become a dominant paradigm for modern visual generation. By progressively transporting noisy latent variables toward structured data samples, they enable impressive image ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) and video synthesis quality ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024a ) . Despite this progress, sampling still requires tens to hundreds of steps, making user-facing applications latency-bound. Figure 1: From forecasting to postdictive smoothing. (a) Forward-only caching commits skipped predictions using historical information and leaves the resulting trajectory drift unrevised. (b) PoSTCache additionally propagates feedback from a later full-computation step backward to retrospectively refine skipped predictions and correct the trajectory. (c) PoSTCache consistently improves the quality–latency trade-off over strong caching baselines across image and video models. Traditional acceleration techniques, such as distillation ( Song et al., 2023 ) and post-training quantization ( Li et al., 2023 ) , often incur additional training costs, architectural modifications, or non-trivial deployment efforts. In contrast, caching provides a lightweight, training-free alternative by exploiting the temporal redundancy of intermediate representations ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Chung et al., 2026 ) . Existing caching approaches have evolved from static feature reuse ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) to adaptive strategies that estimate inter-step redundancy online ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Haghighi and Alahi, 2026 ) , extrapolate future feature trajectories with polynomial approximations ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) , or exploit shallow-layer dynamics to guide deep-layer feature reuse ( Bu et al., 2025 ) . More recently, caching has also been extended beyond the original feature space to spectral representations ( Chung et al., 2026 ) . Despite their diversity, most existing caching methods follow a strictly forward information flow , which we refer to as forecasting : skipped-step predictions are constructed from historical information and committed to the sampling trajectory without later revision, allowing approximation errors to propagate through subsequent updates, as illustrated in Figure 1 (a). This raises a broader question: does later sampling reveal new information that could help correct these earlier errors? In particular, periodic full-computation steps produce fresh predictions after the trajectory has evolved through preceding approximations, potentially exposing backward-looking information about accumulated errors. For example, the discrepancy between a refreshed prediction and its forward proposal can provide such corrective evidence. However, most existing methods use this newly revealed information only for subsequent sampling, rather than propagating it backward to revise earlier estimates. This motivates a postdictive smoothing view of diffusion caching, inspired by Bayesian smoothing, in which later evidence retrospectively revises uncertain intermediate estimates ( Rauch et al., 1965 ; Rabiner, 1989 ; Särkkä and Svensson, 2023 ) . Accordingly, we treat skipped predictions as provisional rather than final, allowing feedback from later full-computation steps to retrospectively refine these estimates and enable backward information flow , as illustrated in Figure 1 (b). Motivated by this perspective, we propose PoSTCache, short for Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache , a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates cache-based acceleration as revisable trajectory inference. Building on an existing caching strategy, PoSTCache propagates feedback from subsequent full-computation anchors backward to refine skipped predictions and reintegrates the corrected trajectory. This shift also changes how anchors should be valued: from their local approximation error to their trajectory-level corrective value. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and greedily selects anchors to reduce surrogate trajectory uncertainty under a fixed computation budget. Figure 1 (c) previews the resulting quality–latency trade-off. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing. We propose PoSTCache, a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching from forward-only forecasting into postdictive smoothing by retrospectively revising skipped predictions. • Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) Anchor Selection. We propose a smoothing-aware PVR strategy that profiles offline denoising trajectories and greedily selects anchors to reduce surrogate trajectory uncertainty under a fixed computation budget. • Superior Performance. Comprehensive experiments across representative image and video models show that PoSTCache improves reconstruction fidelity at comparable or higher acceleration while maintaining competitive semantic generation quality.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Generative Model Acceleration. Acceleration methods for diffusion and flow-based models reduce either the cost of each model evaluation or the number of sampling steps. The former includes model compression techniques such as pruning ( Fang et al., 2023 ) , quantization ( Li et al., 2023 ) , and knowledge distillation ( Meng et al., 2023 ) , as well as computation-efficient designs such as FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) and token reduction ( Bolya et al., 2022 ) . The latter improves sampling efficiency through deterministic sampling with DDIM ( Song et al., 2020a ) , high-order ODE solvers such as DPM-Solver ( Lu et al., 2022 ) , alternative generative dynamics including flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) and rectified flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , or few-step generation through progressive distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) , Shortcut Models ( Frans et al., 2025 ) , and MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2026 ) . Although effective, these approaches often require additional training, architectural changes, or modifications to the sampling process. Cache-based Acceleration. Caching provides a lightweight and training-free alternative by exploiting the temporal redundancy of intermediate representations. Early methods reuse U-Net features with fixed schedules, including DeepCache ( Ma et al., 2024 ) and FasterDiffusion ( Li et al., 2024 ) , while FORA ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) and Δ \Delta -DiT ( Chen et al., 2024b ) extend feature or attention reuse to diffusion transformers. More recent approaches adaptively determine when to refresh cached features using different error proxies, such as TeaCache ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , MagCache ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and DiCache ( Bu et al., 2025 ) . TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025b ) and HiCache ( Feng et al., 2026 ) instead predict future features from historical states. Other methods incorporate trajectory priors, including spectral evolution in SeaCache ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , global path planning in DPCache ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , average-velocity stability in MeanCache ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and offline residual rectification in ERTACache ( Peng et al., 2026 ) . Despite these advances, most methods remain online forward-only: skipped states are determined using historical information or offline priors and remain unrevised after future full-computation states become available. Bayesian Posterior Smoothing. Bayesian smoothing estimates an intermediate latent state using both past and future observations, whereas filtering conditions only on observations available up to the current time. For linear Gaussian systems, this principle underlies Kalman filtering ( Kalman, 1960 ) and the Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother ( Rauch et al., 1965 ) . A similar forward–backward inference procedure is used in hidden Markov models ( Rabiner, 1989 ) . Bayesian smoothing has been generalized to nonlinear and non-Gaussian state-space models ( Särkkä and Svensson, 2023 ) . These methods share the central idea that future evidence can retrospectively correct uncertain intermediate estimates, motivating our reformulation of diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference.

sections.heading: 3.1 Preliminaries
sections.text: Diffusion sampling evolves a latent trajectory through a sequence of model predictions and state updates, resembling sequential Bayesian estimation ( Kalman, 1960 ) . At each denoising step, the model produces a prediction from the information available so far, which is then used by the numerical solver to advance the trajectory. When some predictions are replaced by inaccurate approximations, their errors can propagate through subsequent updates and accumulate along the trajectory. Bayesian smoothing provides a principled mechanism for revising such forward estimates once informative future evidence becomes available ( Rauch et al., 1965 ; Rabiner, 1989 ; Särkkä and Svensson, 2023 ) . Under a linear Gaussian approximation, conditioning the forward estimate at step t t on an observation at a later step b b gives m t | b = m t + P t ​ b ​ ( P b ​ b + R b ) − 1 ​ ( y b − m b ) , m_{t\mid b}=m_{t}+P_{tb}(P_{bb}+R_{b})^{-1}(y_{b}-m_{b}), (1) where y b − m b y_{b}-m_{b} is the future innovation, defined as the residual between the future observation y b y_{b} and its forward prediction m b m_{b} . The factor P t ​ b ​ ( P b ​ b + R b ) − 1 P_{tb}(P_{bb}+R_{b})^{-1} is the smoothing gain. The conditional mean, therefore, takes the generic form smoothed estimate = forward estimate + smoothing gain × future innovation . \text{smoothed estimate}=\text{forward estimate}+\text{smoothing gain}\times\text{future innovation}. (2) This perspective motivates treating skipped diffusion predictions as revisable forward estimates rather than fixed approximations. The sequential-estimation interpretation and the corresponding smoothing derivation are provided in Appendices A.1 and A.2 , respectively. Figure 2: Empirical motivation for postdictive smoothing. (a) Future-anchor residuals increasingly align with preceding proposal errors. (b) The relative-position gain retains over 96% of the explained error achieved by the oracle scalar gain, with a small mean EER gap. (c) Local cache risk is weakly correlated with trajectory-level correction value.

sections.text: Existing caching methods construct skipped predictions from historical states, whose approximation errors are integrated into the sampling trajectory and remain unrevised. Following the Bayesian smoothing interpretation in Sec. 3.1 , we hereafter refer to this residual as the anchor innovation .

sections.text: Figure 2 (c) compares local cache risk with trajectory-level correction value (Appendix C.1 ). sections.heading: 3.3 PoSTCache
sections.text: Motivated by the Bayesian smoothing principle in Sec. 3.1 , which revises a forward estimate using a gain-weighted anchor innovation, and supported by the empirical observations in Sec. 3.2 , PoSTCache uses future-anchor innovations for retrospective trajectory correction and trajectory-level uncertainty for anchor selection, as shown in Figure 3 .

sections.heading: 4.1 Settings
sections.text: Base Models and Compared Methods. We evaluate PoSTCache on three video generation models, Open-Sora 1.2 ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) , CogVideoX ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and Wan 2.1 ( Wan et al., 2025 ) , and two image generation models, FLUX.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) and Qwen-Image-2512 ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . We compare against representative diffusion caching methods, including TeaCache ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , MagCache ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , DiCache ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , HiCache ( Feng et al., 2026 ) , SeaCache ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , and SenCache ( Haghighi and Alahi, 2026 ) . We enable classifier-free guidance (CFG) ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) for Qwen-Image-2512 and Wan 2.1, using identical guidance settings for full inference and all accelerated methods. Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate 200 DrawBench prompts ( Saharia et al., 2022 ) with three random seeds for text-to-image generation and 944 VBench prompts ( Huang et al., 2024 ) with five random seeds for text-to-video generation. Following prior work ( Bu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) , we report latency, speedup, FLOPs, and peak allocated GPU memory. ImageReward and CLIP Score assess image quality, while VBench evaluates video quality. LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , SSIM ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , and PSNR measure reconstruction fidelity against full inference. All results are averaged over random seeds. Implementation Details. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. We use 10 offline calibration trajectories to estimate the cross-timestep covariance statistics. sections.text: Table 3 (a) evaluates the contributions of postdictive smoothing and anchor selection under the same computation budget. Postdictive smoothing consistently improves all three selection strategies, confirming that anchor innovations provide effective corrective information for skipped predictions. sections.text: Table 3 (b) evaluates PoSTCache with MagCache and DiCache as forward caching strategies. sections.heading: Additional Analysis.
sections.text: Appendices C.2 – C.7 further examine calibration-size robustness, validate the PVR objective and schedule transferability, compare alternative global scheduling objectives, and analyze temporal weighting, dense-prefix anchors, and anchor-state consistency. These results support our default design choices, quantify the modest one-time offline calibration cost, and confirm negligible online overhead and favorable quality–efficiency trade-offs.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and Future Work
sections.text: In this work, we presented PoSTCache, a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as a revisable trajectory inference problem. By using feedback from subsequent full-computation steps, PoSTCache retrospectively refines skipped predictions and reintegrates the corrected sampling trajectory. Viewing anchors as sources of corrective feedback, we further introduced a posterior variance reduction criterion to select informative anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty. Extensive experiments on representative image and video generation models demonstrate that PoSTCache consistently improves the efficiency–fidelity trade-off and can be readily integrated with different forward caching strategies. Currently, PoSTCache estimates a shared anchor configuration from offline trajectories and applies it uniformly to all samples. Although this design is simple and effective, it may not fully capture sample-specific trajectory dynamics. A promising direction for future work is to combine the offline uncertainty structure with lightweight online observations, enabling the anchor schedule to adapt to each sampling trajectory without introducing substantial inference overhead.

sections.heading: A.1 Sequential Trajectory Estimation View of Diffusion and Flow Sampling
sections.text: A broad class of diffusion, flow-matching, and rectified-flow samplers can be expressed as a sequence of model predictions and numerical state updates: u k = f θ ​ ( x k , τ k ) , x k + 1 = 𝒮 k ​ ( x k , u k , τ k ) , u_{k}=f_{\theta}(x_{k},\tau_{k}),\qquad x_{k+1}=\mathcal{S}_{k}(x_{k},u_{k},\tau_{k}), (15) where x k x_{k} is the latent state at the k k -th sampling step, τ k \tau_{k} is the corresponding noise or time level, u k u_{k} is the model prediction consumed by the sampler, and 𝒮 k \mathcal{S}_{k} denotes the scheduler or numerical solver. Depending on the model parameterization, u k u_{k} may represent noise, a clean sample estimate, a velocity, or a flow vector. Equation ( 15 ) defines a recursive trajectory estimation process. At each step, the model predicts the local direction of the trajectory from the current latent state, and the solver propagates this prediction to the next state. This structure resembles sequential Bayesian estimation, in which an estimate is repeatedly updated using the information available at the current step. Under cache-based acceleration, some full model predictions are replaced by forward approximations. Let u ~ k = u k − e k \widetilde{u}_{k}=u_{k}-e_{k} (16) denote the cached prediction, where e k e_{k} is the corresponding approximation error. The approximate sampling trajectory then evolves according to x ~ k + 1 = 𝒮 k ​ ( x ~ k , u ~ k , τ k ) . \widetilde{x}_{k+1}=\mathcal{S}_{k}\left(\widetilde{x}_{k},\widetilde{u}_{k},\tau_{k}\right). (17) Because each state is used as the input to subsequent model evaluations and solver updates, an error introduced at one step can affect all later states. To make this propagation explicit, define the latent-state deviation δ ​ x k = x ~ k − x k \delta x_{k}=\widetilde{x}_{k}-x_{k} . A first-order expansion of the solver around the full-computation trajectory gives δ ​ x k + 1 ≈ A k ​ δ ​ x k − B k ​ e k , A k = ∂ 𝒮 k ∂ x k , B k = ∂ 𝒮 k ∂ u k . \delta x_{k+1}\approx A_{k}\delta x_{k}-B_{k}e_{k},\qquad A_{k}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{S}_{k}}{\partial x_{k}},\qquad B_{k}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{S}_{k}}{\partial u_{k}}. (18) Thus, the deviation at step k + 1 k+1 depends not only on the current prediction error but also on the deviation accumulated from previous steps. Repeatedly applying Eq. ( 18 ) over a skipped interval a < k < b a<k<b yields δ x b ≈ A b − 1 ⋯ A a δ x a − ∑ j = a b − 1 ( A b − 1 ⋯ A j + 1 ) B j e j , \delta x_{b}\approx A_{b-1}\cdots A_{a}\delta x_{a}-\sum_{j=a}^{b-1}\left(A_{b-1}\cdots A_{j+1}\right)B_{j}e_{j}, (19) where an empty matrix product is understood as the identity. A complete model evaluation at the current latent state produces u ¯ b = f θ ​ ( x ~ b , τ b ) \bar{u}_{b}=f_{\theta}(\widetilde{x}_{b},\tau_{b}) , while the forward caching rule also provides a proposal u ~ b \widetilde{u}_{b} . Since the preceding cache errors jointly influence the latent state and the forward proposal at step b b , the innovation can contain information about the errors accumulated over the skipped interval. sections.heading: B.2 PoSTCache Configuration
sections.text: PoSTCache consists of a forward proposal strategy, postdictive smoothing and reintegration, and posterior variance reduction anchor selection. Unless otherwise specified, the latest full-computation prediction is reused as the forward proposal. Within each cache interval [ a , b ] [a,b] , the postdictive gain is set to the relative sampling progress w k | a , b = ( η k − η a ) / ( η b − η a ) w_{k\mid a,b}=(\eta_{k}-\eta_{a})/(\eta_{b}-\eta_{a}) . For offline anchor selection, we collect N = 10 N=10 complete denoising trajectories for each model. All non-temporal dimensions are flattened without projection when constructing the cross-timestep covariance kernel. The empirical kernel is normalized by both the number of calibration samples and the trajectory dimension.

sections.heading: Hardware and software.
sections.text: All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU in a Linux environment with Python 3.12.13, CUDA Toolkit 13.0.2, PyTorch 2.11.0, Diffusers 0.37.1, and Transformers 5.4.0. The complete environment configuration and dependency list will be released with the code repository.

sections.heading: Random seeds.
sections.text: We evaluate DrawBench and VBench using three and five different base seeds, respectively, with one sample generated per prompt in each run. Specifically, the image experiments use base seeds { 0 , 2026 , 2027 } \{0,2026,2027\} , while the video experiments use base seeds { 100,200,300,400,500 } \{100,200,300,400,500\} . For a prompt with global index p p , its seed is deterministically assigned as s p = s base + p . s_{p}=s_{\mathrm{base}}+p. (79) Full inference and all accelerated methods use identical prompt–seed pairs, independent of batch size or data-parallel partitioning. Results are averaged over the corresponding base-seed runs.

sections.heading: Latency measurement.
sections.text: Inference latency is measured during the actual generation of the DrawBench and VBench evaluation samples rather than using isolated synthetic inputs. For each prompt–seed pair, wall-clock time is recorded using time.perf_counter() with CUDA synchronization before each timestamp to ensure that asynchronous GPU operations are completed. The reported latency is the arithmetic mean over all evaluated prompts and random seeds for each model and method under the same hardware and software environment. Output serialization and metric computation are excluded from the timing. sections.heading: FLOPs and memory.
sections.text: FLOPs and GPU memory are profiled over the generation loop. FLOPs are estimated using torch.profiler with FLOP counting enabled, and the estimates reported by all supported ATen operators are summed. The profiler primarily provides FLOP metadata for matrix multiplication and convolution; therefore, the reported FLOPs do not necessarily include every element-wise or framework-level operation. Before each profiled generation, we synchronize the GPU and reset the CUDA peak-memory statistics. Peak memory is reported as the maximum allocated CUDA memory obtained from torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() , expressed in GiB. We report allocated rather than reserved memory to reflect the peak memory actively used by tensors during inference.

sections.heading: Offline profiling cost.
sections.text: Offline trajectory collection and anchor selection are performed once for each model. Their costs are excluded from per-sample inference latency because the resulting anchor schedule is shared across all evaluation samples.

sections.heading: B.5 Evaluation Metrics
sections.text: We evaluate both inference efficiency and generation quality. Efficiency is measured by latency, speedup, FLOPs, and peak GPU memory. Generation quality is evaluated using semantic-quality metrics and paired reconstruction metrics.

sections.heading: ImageReward.
sections.text: ImageReward ( Xu et al., 2023 ) is a learned human-preference metric for text-to-image generation. It evaluates the consistency and perceptual quality of a generated image with respect to its text prompt. A higher score indicates stronger alignment with human preference.

sections.heading: CLIP Score.
sections.text: CLIP Score ( Hessel et al., 2021 ) measures text–image alignment using the cosine similarity between pretrained CLIP text and image embeddings. We use the CLIP-ViT-Base-Patch32 model for feature extraction. Higher values indicate stronger semantic consistency with the input prompt.

sections.heading: VBench.
sections.text: VBench ( Huang et al., 2024 ) evaluates video generation along multiple spatial, temporal, semantic, and perceptual dimensions. We use the official evaluation implementation and report its aggregated overall score. Higher scores indicate better video quality.

sections.heading: LPIPS.
sections.text: Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) measures perceptual discrepancy using deep visual features. Let x ^ \hat{x} and x ⋆ x^{\star} denote the accelerated and full-inference outputs, respectively. LPIPS is computed as LPIPS ⁡ ( x ^ , x ⋆ ) = ∑ l 1 H l ​ W l ​ ∑ h , w ‖ 𝐰 l ⊙ ( ϕ ~ l ​ ( x ^ ) h , w − ϕ ~ l ​ ( x ⋆ ) h , w ) ‖ 2 2 , \operatorname{LPIPS}(\hat{x},x^{\star})=\sum_{l}\frac{1}{H_{l}W_{l}}\sum_{h,w}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{l}\odot\left(\widetilde{\phi}_{l}(\hat{x})_{h,w}-\widetilde{\phi}_{l}(x^{\star})_{h,w}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}, (81) where ϕ ~ l ​ ( ⋅ ) \widetilde{\phi}_{l}(\cdot) denotes the channel-normalized feature at layer l l , and 𝐰 l \mathbf{w}_{l} contains the learned channel-wise weights. We use AlexNet as the feature-extraction backbone. Lower values indicate that the accelerated output is perceptually closer to the corresponding full-inference output.

sections.heading: SSIM.
sections.text: Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) ( Wang et al., 2004 ) compares the luminance, contrast, and structural information of the accelerated and full-inference outputs. For two local image windows x ^ \hat{x} and x ⋆ x^{\star} , it is defined as SSIM ⁡ ( x ^ , x ⋆ ) = ( 2 ​ μ x ^ ​ μ x ⋆ + C 1 ) ​ ( 2 ​ σ x ^ ​ x ⋆ + C 2 ) ( μ x ^ 2 + μ x ⋆ 2 + C 1 ) ​ ( σ x ^ 2 + σ x ⋆ 2 + C 2 ) , \operatorname{SSIM}(\hat{x},x^{\star})=\frac{(2\mu_{\hat{x}}\mu_{x^{\star}}+C_{1})(2\sigma_{\hat{x}x^{\star}}+C_{2})}{(\mu_{\hat{x}}^{2}+\mu_{x^{\star}}^{2}+C_{1})(\sigma_{\hat{x}}^{2}+\sigma_{x^{\star}}^{2}+C_{2})}, (82) where μ x ^ \mu_{\hat{x}} and μ x ⋆ \mu_{x^{\star}} are the local means, σ x ^ 2 \sigma_{\hat{x}}^{2} and σ x ⋆ 2 \sigma_{x^{\star}}^{2} are the local variances, σ x ^ ​ x ⋆ \sigma_{\hat{x}x^{\star}} is their covariance, and C 1 C_{1} and C 2 C_{2} are stabilizing constants. The final score is averaged over all spatial windows. Higher values indicate stronger structural similarity.

sections.heading: PSNR.
sections.text: Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio measures pixel-level reconstruction fidelity: PSNR = 10 ​ log 10 ​ ( R 2 MSE ) , \mathrm{PSNR}=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{R^{2}}{\mathrm{MSE}}\right), (83) where R R is the maximum representable pixel value. Higher PSNR indicates smaller pixel-level reconstruction error. For video reconstruction, LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR are computed between temporally corresponding frames and then averaged over frames and evaluation prompts.

sections.heading: C.4 Transferability of Offline PVR Schedules
sections.text: PoSTCache estimates its cross-timestep dependency profile from a small set of offline denoising trajectories and uses the resulting PVR schedule for subsequent inference. We examine whether a schedule profiled in one setting can be reused after changing the prompt distribution, guidance scale, or spatial configuration, without collecting a new target calibration set. For each target setting, we compare two schedules. Transferred directly reuses the schedule selected in the source setting, whereas Reprofiled recomputes the dependency profile from ten target calibration trajectories and reruns the same greedy PVR selector. Both schedules use the same full-computation budget, nearest-reuse proposal, and postdictive smoothing procedure. Each target setting is evaluated against its own full-inference reference. We report the post-smoothing prediction error E post ​ ( A ) E_{\mathrm{post}}(A) defined in Eq. 88 , evaluated on target trajectories disjoint from calibration. This metric measures the discrepancy between corrected model predictions and their full-computation counterparts before accounting for the recursive effect of trajectory reintegration. We additionally report LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR against target full inference to measure the final closed-loop reconstruction quality.

sections.text: The experiments above show that target-specific reprofiling may improve, match, or underperform direct transfer. To identify where these differences arise, we use three complementary diagnostics. First, profile similarity measures whether the source and target settings exhibit similar relative cross-timestep dependency patterns. Let K ( s ) K^{(s)} and K ( t ) K^{(t)} denote the covariance kernels estimated from the source and target calibration trajectories, respectively, using Eq. 100 . Since their marginal prediction variances may differ across settings, we first convert each covariance kernel into a correlation profile: C i ​ j ( x ) = K i ​ j ( x ) max ⁡ ( K i ​ i ( x ) , ϵ ) ​ max ⁡ ( K j ​ j ( x ) , ϵ ) , x ∈ { s , t } , C^{(x)}_{ij}=\frac{K^{(x)}_{ij}}{\sqrt{\max\!\left(K^{(x)}_{ii},\epsilon\right)\max\!\left(K^{(x)}_{jj},\epsilon\right)}},\qquad x\in\{s,t\}, (90) where ϵ = 10 − 12 \epsilon=10^{-12} is used for numerical stability. Let 𝐜 ( x ) = vec i < j ⁡ ( C i ​ j ( x ) ) \mathbf{c}^{(x)}=\operatorname{vec}_{i<j}\left(C^{(x)}_{ij}\right) (91) denote the vector containing the strictly upper-triangular entries of C ( x ) C^{(x)} . We define profile similarity as the Pearson correlation between the source and target profile vectors: Sim profile = ∑ k ( c k ( s ) − c ¯ ( s ) ) ​ ( c k ( t ) − c ¯ ( t ) ) ∑ k ( c k ( s ) − c ¯ ( s ) ) 2 ​ ∑ k ( c k ( t ) − c ¯ ( t ) ) 2 . \operatorname{Sim}_{\mathrm{profile}}=\frac{\sum_{k}\left(c_{k}^{(s)}-\bar{c}^{(s)}\right)\left(c_{k}^{(t)}-\bar{c}^{(t)}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum_{k}\left(c_{k}^{(s)}-\bar{c}^{(s)}\right)^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{k}\left(c_{k}^{(t)}-\bar{c}^{(t)}\right)^{2}}}. A value close to one indicates that the source and target profiles exhibit similar relative cross-timestep dependency patterns, even when their absolute covariance magnitudes or marginal variances differ. sections.heading: Comparison with DPCache.
sections.text: PVR globally models cross-timestep dependencies when evaluating the information value of an anchor. DPCache ( Cui et al., 2026 ) is therefore the closest conceptual comparison, as it also formulates timestep selection as a global optimization problem, but minimizes a path-additive cost through dynamic programming. To isolate the scheduling objective, we adapt DPCache to the same PoSTCache online pipeline. DPCache-Pre follows the original pre-correction principle and constructs its path cost from nearest-reuse proposal errors before postdictive smoothing. DPCache-Retro is our correction-aware extension, which retains the same dynamic-programming formulation but computes the interval cost after applying postdictive smoothing. All selectors use FLUX.1-dev with 50 sampling steps, a budget of B = 16 B=16 , ten calibration trajectories, and the same nearest-reuse and single-anchor smoothing pipeline. Prediction-space evaluation uses ten disjoint held-out trajectories, while reconstruction metrics are evaluated over 200 prompts. Table 17: Comparison with path-based scheduling on FLUX.1-dev. DPCache-Retro is our correction-aware extension of DPCache. All selectors use the same online pipeline and computation budget. DPCache-Retro obtains a slightly lower held-out E post E_{\mathrm{post}} than PVR, which is expected because its path cost is directly constructed from the post-smoothing prediction error. Nevertheless, PVR achieves the best final reconstruction quality across all three metrics. This discrepancy further reflects the offline–online gap: reducing prediction error on stored full-computation trajectories does not fully capture how reintegration changes the latent trajectory and recursively affects later model predictions. It also highlights the distinction between the two global objectives: DPCache minimizes fixed path-additive interval costs, whereas PVR evaluates the uncertainty reduction of each anchor conditioned on the complete selected set, thereby modeling redundancy and complementarity among anchors.

sections.heading: C.8 Additional Qualitative Results
sections.text: We provide additional qualitative comparisons to complement the image results in the main paper. The examples cover diverse prompts, model architectures, and acceleration regimes. Across these settings, PoSTCache more closely follows full inference in terms of global composition, local appearance, and object structure. For video generation, it additionally reduces structural and appearance deviations across the sampled frames, while achieving acceleration ratios comparable to or higher than those of the competing methods.

sections.heading: Qwen-Image-2512.
sections.text: Figure 8 presents additional text-to-image results on Qwen-Image-2512. At a 2.90 × 2.90\times speedup, PoSTCache closely preserves both the global layout and fine-grained structures of full inference. In the fireworks example, it retains the shapes of the rendered letters and the local burst patterns. In the moonlit cat and industrial landscape examples, it better preserves small foreground elements, cloud boundaries, vegetation, and reflection details. In comparison, competing methods tend to smooth away these local structures or introduce more noticeable changes in color, illumination, and scene layout. These results indicate that postdictive correction mitigates not only semantic degradation but also the accumulation of fine-grained appearance errors. Figure 8: Qualitative comparison with previous acceleration methods on Qwen-Image-2512.

sections.heading: OpenSora 1.2.
sections.text: Figure 9 compares PoSTCache with representative caching methods on OpenSora 1.2. PoSTCache more faithfully preserves object identity, geometry, and prompt-specified spatial relationships across the sampled frames. For example, it maintains the contour and proportions of the pink vase, the relative arrangement of the couch and bed, and the left–right relationship between the toothbrush and hair drier. TeaCache and MagCache, by contrast, produce more visible changes in object shape, orientation, or relative placement. The improvements are obtained at a comparable acceleration ratio, suggesting that retrospective correction is effective for preventing structural deviations from propagating along the video trajectory. sections.heading: CogVideoX.
sections.text: Figure 10 further evaluates PoSTCache on CogVideoX using stylized landscapes, natural scenes, and architectural objects. PoSTCache closely reproduces the object scale and scene composition of full inference, including the position of the Eiffel Tower and boat, the appearance of the lakeside bench, and the silhouette of the Gothic-style lamppost. Moreover, these structures remain comparatively stable across the displayed frames. TeaCache and SenCache exhibit larger variations in object proportions, background layout, or foreground appearance. This comparison demonstrates that PoSTCache remains effective when the underlying model architecture and visual content differ substantially from those of OpenSora. Figure 10: Qualitative comparison with previous acceleration methods on CogVideoX.

sections.heading: Wan 2.1.
sections.text: Figure 11 shows the corresponding comparisons on Wan 2.1. The selected prompts test both compositional relationships and the preservation of distinctive scene structures. For the boat–airplane example, PoSTCache maintains the prompt-specified relative positions and closely follows the full-inference object silhouettes. For the lighthouse and castle examples, it preserves the principal architectural structures, surrounding vegetation, and overall scene appearance across frames. DiCache introduces substantial structural degradation in the lighthouse scene, while SenCache produces more noticeable changes in object geometry and background appearance. PoSTCache therefore provides a closer approximation to full inference while attaining the highest acceleration ratio among the compared methods in this setting. Figure 11: Qualitative comparison with previous acceleration methods on Wan 2.1. Overall, the qualitative results are consistent with the reconstruction metrics reported in the main paper. By revising skipped predictions using future-anchor evidence, PoSTCache reduces accumulated errors in local texture, object geometry, spatial composition, and temporal appearance across different image and video generation architectures.

sections.heading: C.9 Limitations and Boundary Conditions
sections.text: PoSTCache relies on offline trajectory statistics to construct a shared anchor schedule. The resulting schedule transfers well across the evaluated prompt distributions, guidance scales, and spatial configurations, but this does not imply that the underlying dependency profile is invariant or that a single schedule is optimal for every sample. Target-specific reprofiling can improve the offline PVR objective or the held-out prediction-space error without improving the final reconstruction. This discrepancy reflects an offline–online gap: the offline profile is estimated on stored full-computation trajectories, whereas online correction changes the latent states and recursively affects subsequent model predictions. In addition, the current greedy selector is path dependent; small finite-sample perturbations of otherwise similar covariance profiles can alter early anchor choices and produce substantially different schedules. Combining the shared offline prior with inexpensive online trajectory observations is therefore a promising direction for more stable and sample-adaptive anchor selection. Retrospective reintegration can also introduce a local state–prediction mismatch at future anchors. Appendix C.6 shows that unconditional anchor refresh reduces this mismatch but is less compute-efficient than broader anchor coverage in our matched-NFE comparison. Our analysis nevertheless compares only two coarse allocation strategies and does not exclude more selective policies. An adaptive scheme that refreshes only high-risk anchors, or dynamically allocates each additional model evaluation between anchor refresh and new anchor placement, may yield a more favorable consistency–coverage trade-off. Postdictive correction further relies on the temporal correlation between skipped prediction errors and innovations revealed by future anchors. Our implementation approximates the full covariance-dependent smoothing gain with an isotropic linear gain determined by sampling progress. Although this approximation is effective in the evaluated regimes, it cannot fully capture nonlinear, feature-dependent, or sample-specific error evolution. Under very aggressive acceleration or unusually long cache intervals, accumulated drift may weaken the relationship between a future innovation and earlier skipped predictions, limiting the recoverable error.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.25664v1 [cs.CV] 19 Oct 2026 PoSTCache: From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing for Revisable Diffusion Caching Liwei Lan Email: llw25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn Hui Chen Affiliation: School of Software, Tsinghua University BNRist, Tsinghua University Email: huichen@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn Jungong Han Affiliation: Department of Automation, Tsinghua University Email: jghan@tsinghua.edu.cn Guiguang Ding Email: dinggg@tsinghua.edu.cn Abstract Diffusion and flow matching models achieve impressive visual generation quality but remain computationally expensive due to iterative sampling. Caching-based acceleration provides a practical training-free solution by reusing or predicting intermediate features. However, existing methods largely enforce a forward-only information flow: approximations produced for skipped model evaluations are immediately committed to the sampling trajectory and cannot benefit from feedback generated by later full-computation steps. We propose PoSTCache ( Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache ), a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. PoSTCache first uses an existing caching strategy to construct forward proposals for skipped steps. At a later full-computation step, the discrepancy between the refreshed prediction and its forward proposal yields a correction signal, which PoSTCache propagates backward to refine and reintegrate the preceding predictions. Viewing full-computation steps as sources of corrective feedback also changes how they should be selected. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and selects anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty rather than local approximation error alone. Experiments on representative image and video generation models show that PoSTCache consistently improves the quality–efficiency trade-off over representative caching methods. 1 Introduction Diffusion models ( Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020b ) and flow matching models ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) have become a dominant paradigm for modern visual generation. By progressively transporting noisy latent variables toward structured data samples, they enable impressive image ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2024 ) and video synthesis quality ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024a ) . Despite this progress, sampling still requires tens to hundreds of steps, making user-facing applications latency-bound. Figure 1: From forecasting to postdictive smoothing. (a) Forward-only caching commits skipped predictions using historical information and leaves the resulting trajectory drift unrevised. (b) PoSTCache additionally propagates feedback from a later full-computation step backward to retrospectively refine skipped predictions and correct the trajectory. (c) PoSTCache consistently improves the quality–latency trade-off over strong caching baselines across image and video models. Traditional acceleration techniques, such as distillation ( Song et al., 2023 ) and post-training quantization ( Li et al., 2023 ) , often incur additional training costs, architectural modifications, or non-trivial deployment efforts. In contrast, caching provides a lightweight, training-free alternative by exploiting the temporal redundancy of intermediate representations ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Chung et al., 2026 ) . Existing caching approaches have evolved from static feature reuse ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) to adaptive strategies that estimate inter-step redundancy online ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Haghighi and Alahi, 2026 ) , extrapolate future feature trajectories with polynomial approximations ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) , or exploit shallow-layer dynamics to guide deep-layer feature reuse ( Bu et al., 2025 ) . More recently, caching has also been extended beyond the original feature space to spectral representations ( Chung et al., 2026 ) . Despite their diversity, most existing caching methods follow a strictly forward information flow , which we refer to as forecasting : skipped-step predictions are constructed from historical information and committed to the sampling trajectory without later revision, allowing approximation errors to propagate through subsequent updates, as illustrated in Figure 1 (a). This raises a broader question: does later sampling reveal new information that could help correct these earlier errors? In particular, periodic full-computation steps produce fresh predictions after the trajectory has evolved through preceding approximations, potentially exposing backward-looking information about accumulated errors. For example, the discrepancy between a refreshed prediction and its forward proposal can provide such corrective evidence. However, most existing methods use this newly revealed information only for subsequent sampling, rather than propagating it backward to revise earlier estimates. This motivates a postdictive smoothing view of diffusion caching, inspired by Bayesian smoothing, in which later evidence retrospectively revises uncertain intermediate estimates ( Rauch et al., 1965 ; Rabiner, 1989 ; Särkkä and Svensson, 2023 ) . Accordingly, we treat skipped predictions as provisional rather than final, allowing feedback from later full-computation steps to retrospectively refine these estimates and enable backward information flow , as illustrated in Figure 1 (b). Motivated by this perspective, we propose PoSTCache, short for Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache , a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates cache-based acceleration as revisable trajectory inference. Building on an existing caching strategy, PoSTCache propagates feedback from subsequent full-computation anchors backward to refine skipped predictions and reintegrates the corrected trajectory. This shift also changes how anchors should be valued: from their local approximation error to their trajectory-level corrective value. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and greedily selects anchors to reduce surrogate trajectory uncertainty under a fixed computation budget. Figure 1 (c) previews the resulting quality–latency trade-off. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing. We propose PoSTCache, a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching from forward-only forecasting into postdictive smoothing by retrospectively revising skipped predictions. • Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) Anchor Selection. We propose a smoothing-aware PVR strategy that profiles offline denoising trajectories and greedily selects anchors to reduce surrogate trajectory uncertainty under a fixed computation budget. • Superior Performance. Comprehensive experiments across representative image and video models show that PoSTCache improves reconstruction fidelity at comparable or higher acceleration while maintaining competitive semantic generation quality. 2 Related Work Generative Model Acceleration. Acceleration methods for diffusion and flow-based models reduce either the cost of each model evaluation or the number of sampling steps. The former includes model compression techniques such as pruning ( Fang et al., 2023 ) , quantization ( Li et al., 2023 ) , and knowledge distillation ( Meng et al., 2023 ) , as well as computation-efficient designs such as FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) and token reduction ( Bolya et al., 2022 ) . The latter improves sampling efficiency through deterministic sampling with DDIM ( Song et al., 2020a ) , high-order ODE solvers such as DPM-Solver ( Lu et al., 2022 ) , alternative generative dynamics including flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) and rectified flow ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , or few-step generation through progressive distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) , Shortcut Models ( Frans et al., 2025 ) , and MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2026 ) . Although effective, these approaches often require additional training, architectural changes, or modifications to the sampling process. Cache-based Acceleration. Caching provides a lightweight and training-free alternative by exploiting the temporal redundancy of intermediate representations. Early methods reuse U-Net features with fixed schedules, including DeepCache ( Ma et al., 2024 ) and FasterDiffusion ( Li et al., 2024 ) , while FORA ( Selvaraju et al., 2024 ) and Δ \Delta -DiT ( Chen et al., 2024b ) extend feature or attention reuse to diffusion transformers. More recent approaches adaptively determine when to refresh cached features using different error proxies, such as TeaCache ( Liu et al., 2025a ) , MagCache ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and DiCache ( Bu et al., 2025 ) . TaylorSeer ( Liu et al., 2025b ) and HiCache ( Feng et al., 2026 ) instead predict future features from historical states. Other methods incorporate trajectory priors, including spectral evolution in SeaCache ( Chung et al., 2026 ) , global path planning in DPCache ( Cui et al., 2026 ) , average-velocity stability in MeanCache ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and offline residual rectification in ERTACache ( Peng et al., 2026 ) . Despite these advances, most methods remain online forward-only: skipped states are determined using historical information or offline priors and remain unrevised after future full-computation states become available. Bayesian Posterior Smoothing. Bayesian smoothing estimates an intermediate latent state using both past and future observations, whereas filtering conditions only on observations available up to the current time. For linear Gaussian systems, this principle underlies Kalman filtering ( Kalman, 1960 ) and the Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother ( Rauch et al., 1965 ) . A similar forward–backward inference procedure is used in hidden Markov models ( Rabiner, 1989 ) . Bayesian smoothing has been generalized to nonlinear and non-Gaussian state-space models ( Särkkä and Svensson, 2023 ) . These methods share the central idea that future evidence can retrospectively correct uncertain intermediate estimates, motivating our reformulation of diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. 3 Method 3.1 Preliminaries Diffusion sampling evolves a latent trajectory through a sequence of model predictions and state updates, resembling sequential Bayesian estimation ( Kalman, 1960 ) . Appendices C.2 – C.7 further examine calibration-size robustness, validate the PVR objective and schedule transferability, compare alternative global scheduling objectives, and analyze temporal weighting, dense-prefix anchors, and anchor-state consistency. These results support our default design choices, quantify the modest one-time offline calibration cost, and confirm negligible online overhead and favorable quality–efficiency trade-offs. 5 Conclusion and Future Work In this work, we presented PoSTCache, a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as a revisable trajectory inference problem. By using feedback from subsequent full-computation steps, PoSTCache retrospectively refines skipped predictions and reintegrates the corrected sampling trajectory. Viewing anchors as sources of corrective feedback, we further introduced a posterior variance reduction criterion to select informative anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty. Extensive experiments on representative image and video generation models demonstrate that PoSTCache consistently improves the efficiency–fidelity trade-off and can be readily integrated with different forward caching strategies. Currently, PoSTCache estimates a shared anchor configuration from offline trajectories and applies it uniformly to all samples. Although this design is simple and effective, it may not fully capture sample-specific trajectory dynamics. A promising direction for future work is to combine the offline uncertainty structure with lightweight online observations, enabling the anchor schedule to adapt to each sampling trajectory without introducing substantial inference overhead.
